tool.name: Spring Boot
tool.tagline: Opinionated Java framework for production-ready web services and apps
tool.description: Spring Boot builds on the Spring Framework to create stand-alone, production-ready Java applications with minimal configuration: starters pull in consistent dependencies, auto-configuration wires sensible defaults, and an embedded server runs the app as a plain jar. It is the most widely used way to build REST APIs, microservices and data-backed backends on the JVM. Learning it means learning dependency injection, Spring MVC, Spring Data, testing and operations the way most Java teams practise them.

glossary.def: A Java framework for building server programs, especially web APIs. It builds on the Spring Framework and sets most things up for you with sensible defaults.
Short for Spring Boot, the Java framework for building server programs and web APIs with sensible defaults.
The older, larger Java framework underneath Spring Boot. It creates and connects your objects (beans) and provides web, data and security features.
The website start.spring.io (also built into IDEs) that generates a ready-to-run Spring Boot project with the dependencies you pick.
In Spring Boot, one dependency that brings in a tested set of libraries for one job, such as spring-boot-starter-web for web APIs.
A web server that runs inside your own application, so the app is one program you start with java -jar rather than something installed into a separate server.
A widely used Java web server. Spring Boot's web starter runs it inside your app as the embedded server.
Spring's web layer: it receives HTTP requests, calls the matching controller method and turns the result into the response.
The library Spring Boot uses to turn Java objects into JSON text and JSON back into objects.
An object that Spring creates, configures and hands to the other objects that need it, instead of your code calling new.
Spring's central object that creates all the beans, connects them to each other and manages them while the app runs. Also called the IoC (inversion of control) container.
Spring Boot setting up beans for you based on which libraries are on the classpath and your settings, e.g. a web server when the web starter is present.
Spring searching the main class's package and its sub-packages for classes marked @Component, @Service, @RestController and similar, and making beans of them.
An annotation that marks a class as a bean and says its role: @Component in general, @Service for business logic, @Repository for data access, @Controller for web.
Spring passing a bean the objects it needs as constructor arguments. The recommended way to receive dependencies.
Spring setting a dependency directly into a field marked @Autowired. It works but hides what a class needs, so constructor injection is preferred.
In Spring Boot, a named setting such as server.port=8081, read from application.properties, environment variables or the command line.
A named set of settings and beans, such as dev or prod, that applies only when that profile is active (e.g. SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod).
spring-boot-devtools: a development-only dependency that restarts your app automatically when you recompile.
One JAR file containing your classes, all their dependencies and a launcher, so the app runs anywhere with java -jar.
The most widely used tool for building container images and running containers.
A system that runs containers across many machines, restarting them when they fail and starting more copies when needed.
Data transfer object: a simple class or record that only carries data into or out of your API, kept separate from your database classes.
Jakarta Persistence: Java's standard way to map classes to database tables, so you save and load objects and the library writes the SQL.
The most widely used JPA implementation, and the one Spring Boot uses: it turns your entity objects into SQL and back.
A Spring library that writes database access code for you: you declare a repository interface and it provides the implementation.
A class annotated @Entity whose objects are stored as rows of a database table, one field per column.
In Spring Data, an interface such as BookRepository extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> for which Spring writes the database code: save, find, delete and queries.
A Spring Data repository method whose query is built from its name, such as findByAuthor(String author).
Jakarta Persistence Query Language: a SQL-like query language that uses your entity class and field names instead of table and column names.
Java's standard way to talk to relational databases. Each database supplies a JDBC driver library that does the actual talking.
A numbered script that changes the database's structure one step (e.g. adds a column). Tools like Flyway and Liquibase apply them in order, once each.
Hibernate noticing that a loaded entity's fields were changed and writing the change to the database automatically when the transaction ends.
In Spring, a stand-in object wrapped around your bean. Other beans call the proxy, which runs extra behaviour (start a transaction, run in the background) around your method.
In Spring, how many instances of a bean exist and for how long: singleton (one per app, the default), prototype (new each time), request or session.
A Spring test tool that sends fake HTTP requests to your controllers without starting a real server, and checks the responses.
The common Java library for mocks: fake objects whose answers you program in a test, e.g. when(service.find(1)).thenReturn(book).
A Spring Boot test that starts only one layer of the app, such as the web layer with @WebMvcTest, so it runs faster than starting everything.
Spring's class for the standard JSON error format (RFC 9457): fields type, title, status, detail and instance, plus your own.
A Java interface whose methods are annotated with @GetExchange and similar; Spring generates a client that sends the matching HTTP requests.
Spring's modern HTTP client for calling other web APIs from your code, with a fluent style: client.get().uri(...).retrieve().body(Type.class).
Spring Boot Actuator: adds ready-made endpoints under /actuator to check the app's health, read its metrics and inspect its setup.
A small check of one thing the app depends on, such as the database, reported as UP or DOWN at /actuator/health.
The library Spring Boot uses to record metrics (counters, timers) and send them to monitoring systems like Prometheus.
A popular monitoring system that regularly collects metrics from your services and stores them so you can graph them and raise alerts.
In web security, a signed string a client sends with each request to prove who it is and what it may do, instead of a username and password.
The list of security checks (filters) every request passes through in Spring Security before reaching your controllers; you configure it as a bean.
Loading a list with one query and then running one more query for each item, often by accident, so 100 items cost 101 queries.
A JPQL query part (join fetch) that loads related objects in the same query, instead of one extra query each later.
A query result that holds only selected fields (as a record or interface) instead of whole entities; cheaper for read-only screens.
A Spring Boot default that keeps the database session open until the web response is written, so related data can still load in controllers.
A Java library that starts real services such as PostgreSQL in throwaway Docker containers for tests, and removes them afterwards.
Aspect-oriented programming: adding behaviour (timing, transactions, security) around many methods from one place, done in Spring with proxies.
Ahead-of-time processing: Spring doing at build time the setup work it would normally do at startup, generating code that starts faster.
A program compiled by GraalVM straight to machine code for one operating system, with no JVM needed; it starts in milliseconds.
Class Data Sharing: a JVM feature that saves already-loaded classes to a file, so later starts of the same app are faster.
A startup report (printed with --debug) listing which auto-configurations Spring Boot applied or skipped, and why.
In Java, a named group of related classes, like a folder, such as com.example.shop. Its name matches the folder the files are in.

concepts.name: How web services talk: HTTP and JSON
concepts.summary: The few web ideas every Spring Boot app relies on: clients and servers, requests and responses, URLs, ports, status codes and JSON.
concepts.why: A Spring Boot web app answers HTTP requests all day; every later lesson assumes these words.
concepts.body:
When you open a weather app, it asks a computer somewhere for today's forecast and shows the answer. The program that asks is the **client**. The program that waits for questions and answers them is the **server**. Most of what you build with Spring Boot is a server: a program that keeps running and answers other programs.

They talk using **HTTP**, the same rules web browsers use. Every exchange is one **request** from the client followed by one **response** from the server, like a letter and its reply.

A request says where it is going with a **URL**, a web address such as `http://localhost:8080/api/books/7`. The last part, `/api/books/7`, is the path: which thing you want.

`localhost` is the name your computer uses for itself, handy while developing. `8080` is the **port**: a numbered door on that computer, so several servers can run side by side, each listening at its own number.

Anything after a `?`, as in `/api/books?page=2`, is the **query string**: extra `name=value` options for the request.

Each request also has an **HTTP method**, a verb saying what to do: **GET** reads something, **POST** creates something new, `PUT` replaces it, `PATCH` changes part of it, and `DELETE` removes it.

Every response starts with a **status code**, a three-digit number saying how it went: `200` OK, `201` created, `204` done with nothing to send back, `400` the request was wrong, `404` not found, `500` the server failed. Codes in the 400s mean the client made a mistake; 500s mean the server did.

The data itself travels in the **request body** (or response body), usually as **JSON**: a text format for structured data, like `{"id": 7, "title": "Dune"}`. Names are in quotes, values follow a colon, and `[ ]` holds a list.

Requests and responses also carry **headers**, extra `Name: value` lines. `Content-Type: application/json` says the body is JSON.

A program that offers operations to other programs is an **API**; one reached over HTTP is a **web API**. Each method-plus-path it answers, like `GET /api/books/7`, is an **endpoint**. The `curl` command lets you call any endpoint from a terminal.
concepts.code:
# GET: read book 7 (-i also prints the status line and headers)
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/books/7
# HTTP/1.1 200
# Content-Type: application/json
#
# {"id":7,"title":"Dune","author":"Herbert"}

# POST: create a book, sending JSON in the request body
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/books \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"title":"Emma","author":"Austen"}'
# HTTP/1.1 201
# Location: http://localhost:8080/api/books/8

# A book that doesn't exist
curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/books/999
# HTTP/1.1 404
takeaways: A client sends a request; a server sends back a response
A request has a method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and a URL
The status code says how it went: 2xx success, 4xx client mistake, 5xx server failure
Data travels as JSON in the body; headers describe it
pitfalls: Treating every error as the server's fault: a 4xx status means the request itself needs fixing.

quiz.q: A client asks GET /api/books/42 and no such book exists. Which status code fits best?
quiz.explain: 404 Not Found says the thing asked for doesn't exist; 500 would mean the server itself broke.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method should a client use to create a new book?
quiz.explain: POST creates something new; GET only reads and DELETE removes.

concepts.name: Creating a Spring Boot app
concepts.summary: Generate a project with Spring Initializr, understand starters and @SpringBootApplication, and run your first web server.
concepts.why: Every Spring Boot project starts from this structure, and knowing what each piece does takes the mystery out of the framework.
concepts.body:
**Spring Boot** is a framework for building server programs in Java, especially web APIs. It builds on the older **Spring Framework** and adds sensible defaults, so a working server takes only a few lines.

The quickest start is **Spring Initializr** (start.spring.io, also built into IntelliJ and VS Code). Pick Maven or Gradle and Java 17 or newer (21 is a good choice), and add dependencies such as *Spring Web*. You download a ready project with a build file, a main class, a settings file called `application.properties`, and a test.

Dependencies come as **starters**: one dependency that brings in a tested set of libraries for one job. Spring Boot also fixes compatible versions of all these libraries, so you rarely write a version number yourself.

`spring-boot-starter-web` brings **Spring MVC**, Spring's web layer, and **Jackson**, which turns Java objects into JSON and back. It also brings **Tomcat**, a web server that runs inside your app: an **embedded server**, so your app is one program you start, not something you install into a server.

The main class is annotated `@SpringBootApplication`. In Spring, a **bean** is an object Spring creates and manages for you (the next lesson covers them). The annotation combines three things:

- `@Configuration`: this class may define beans.
- `@EnableAutoConfiguration`: turns on **auto-configuration**. Spring Boot looks at which libraries are on the classpath and sets up matching beans; Tomcat and Spring MVC get set up because the web starter is there.
- `@ComponentScan`: turns on **component scanning**. Spring searches this class's package **and its sub-packages** for classes marked `@Component`, `@Service`, `@RestController` and similar, and makes beans of them.

`SpringApplication.run(App.class, args)` creates the **application context**, the object that holds all the beans, then starts the embedded server on port 8080 and keeps running until you stop it. Put the main class in a top-level package such as `com.example.shop`, so scanning finds everything below it.
takeaways: Starters bundle a tested set of dependencies; Boot manages their versions
`@SpringBootApplication` = configuration + auto-configuration + component scanning
Component scanning covers the main class's package and its sub-packages
The embedded server makes the app one self-contained program
pitfalls: Putting the main class in a sub-package, so controllers in sibling packages are never scanned.

quiz.q: Why is a @RestController in com.example.web not found when the main class is in com.example.app?
options: Controllers must be in the same file
@RestController needs to be registered in application.properties
Component scanning starts at the main class's package and only covers its sub-packages
quiz.explain: @SpringBootApplication scans its own package downwards; com.example.web is a sibling, not a sub-package.

concepts.name: Beans and dependency injection
concepts.summary: Let Spring create your objects (beans) and hand each one the other objects it needs through its constructor.
concepts.why: This hand-over, called dependency injection, is the core of Spring; every other feature is built on beans.
concepts.body:
In plain Java, a class that needs another object creates it: `SignupService` calls `new EmailNotifier()` itself. The two are now welded together. To test `SignupService` with a fake notifier, or to switch to text messages, you have to edit it.

Spring turns this around. You declare your classes, and the application context creates one of each, as beans, and connects them. Because Spring rather than your code is in control of creating objects, the application context is also called the **IoC container** (inversion of control). Handing an object what it needs from outside is called **dependency injection**.

Two ways to declare beans:

- Mark a class with `@Component` or a more descriptive **stereotype**: `@Service` for business logic, `@Repository` for data access, `@RestController` for web endpoints. Component scanning finds it.
- Write a `@Bean` method in a `@Configuration` class that returns the object. Use this for classes from libraries, which you can't annotate, or for objects that need special setup.

Spring passes dependencies in through the constructor; this is **constructor injection**. Declare a `final` field and a constructor parameter of that type, and Spring supplies the matching bean. With a single constructor you need no annotation. Dependencies are visible, fields can be final, and tests can build the class with plain `new` and fake parts. **Field injection** (`@Autowired` on a field) still works but hides what a class needs; avoid it.

Depend on interfaces where it helps: inject `PaymentGateway`, not `StripeGateway`. If several beans implement the interface, mark the default one `@Primary`, pick one by name with `@Qualifier("name")`, or inject `List<PaymentGateway>` to get them all.

By default each bean is a **singleton**: Spring makes one instance and shares it everywhere. A web server handles many requests at once on different threads, all using that same instance. So beans must not keep per-request data in fields: keep them **stateless** (fields hold only other beans and settings) or make them thread-safe.
takeaways: Spring creates beans and injects the dependencies they need
Use stereotypes for your own classes and `@Bean` methods for library objects
Prefer constructor injection with final fields
Beans are singletons by default, so keep them stateless
pitfalls: Storing per-request data in a field of a singleton @Service, which is shared across all requests.

quiz.q: A @Service has one constructor taking a Notifier. What do you need for Spring to inject it?
options: Nothing: a single constructor is used automatically
quiz.explain: Since Spring 4.3, the only constructor of a bean is used for injection without any annotation.

concepts.name: application.properties and @Value
concepts.summary: Configure your app and Spring Boot's own parts in application.properties (or YAML), and read your own settings with @Value.
concepts.why: Keeping settings outside the code lets the same JAR run on your laptop, in testing and for real users.
takeaways: `application.properties` (or `.yml`) configures Boot and your own code
Environment variables and command-line arguments override packaged values
`@Value("${key:default}")` injects one value
Keep secrets out of files stored with the code
pitfalls: Hard-coding environment-specific addresses in the JAR instead of overriding them per environment.

quiz.q: application.properties sets server.port=8080 and the environment has SERVER_PORT=9000. Which port is used?
quiz.explain: Environment variables have higher precedence than packaged properties, and relaxed binding maps SERVER_PORT to server.port.

concepts.name: Building and running the jar
concepts.summary: Run your app while developing, bundle it as one runnable JAR, and restart quickly with DevTools.
concepts.why: You need a fast loop while coding and a single file to ship.
concepts.body:
The Spring Boot build **plugin**, an add-on for Maven or Gradle, does two jobs. While developing, `./mvnw spring-boot:run` (or `./gradlew bootRun`) compiles and starts the app straight from your project.

To ship it, `./mvnw package` (or `./gradlew bootJar`) builds a **fat JAR** in `target/`: one JAR holding your classes, every dependency JAR and a small launcher. Any computer with a JVM runs it with `java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar`; nothing else needs installing, because the server is inside.

Use the wrapper scripts (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) that Initializr generates, so everyone builds with the same Maven or Gradle version.

**DevTools** (`spring-boot-devtools`, a dependency used only while developing) restarts the app automatically when you recompile, which is much faster than stopping and starting it yourself. It is left out of the packaged JAR automatically.

Many teams run apps in **containers**: sealed-off bundles holding an app and everything it needs, which start in moments on any machine. The usual tool for them is **Docker**. `./mvnw spring-boot:build-image` builds such a bundle, a **container image**, without you writing a Dockerfile (Docker's recipe file).

If you do write your own Dockerfile, let Boot split the JAR into layers (`java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers`), so unchanged dependencies are reused between builds instead of copied again.

At startup the log shows the port and how long startup took. Add `--debug` to print the **auto-configuration report**: what Boot set up and why, useful when something isn't configured the way you expect.
concepts.code:
# development
./mvnw spring-boot:run                      # or: ./gradlew bootRun

# package an executable jar and run it
./mvnw clean package
java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --server.port=9090

# container image via buildpacks (needs Docker)
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=shop:latest
docker run -p 8080:8080 shop:latest

# see why things were (not) auto-configured
java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --debug | grep -A3 "Positive matches"
takeaways: `spring-boot:run`/`bootRun` while developing, `package`/`bootJar` for a fat JAR
The fat JAR runs anywhere with `java -jar`
DevTools restarts on change and is left out of the packaged JAR
`build-image` creates a container image without a Dockerfile
pitfalls: Shipping the plain JAR without the Boot plugin's repackaging: it lacks the dependencies and fails with ClassNotFoundException.

quiz.q: What makes the Spring Boot jar executable with java -jar?
options: The plugin repackages it with all dependencies and a launcher main class
quiz.explain: The Boot plugin repackages the JAR with the dependency JARs inside it and a launcher that finds them.

concepts.name: REST controllers and request mapping
concepts.summary: Map HTTP requests to Java methods with @RestController, @GetMapping, @PathVariable and @RequestParam.
concepts.why: Web APIs in the REST style are the most common thing built with Spring Boot.
concepts.body:
A **REST** API is the usual style of web API: URLs name things (resources such as `/api/books/7`), and HTTP methods say what to do with them. In Spring, a class annotated `@RestController` answers such requests.

Each method's return value becomes the response body. Jackson **serializes** it: turns the Java object into JSON text. `@RequestMapping("/api/books")` on the class sets a path prefix shared by all its methods.

Methods are mapped with `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping` and `@DeleteMapping`, one per HTTP method. Method parameters pick parts out of the request:

- `@PathVariable Long id` takes `{id}` from the path `/api/books/{id}` and converts it to the declared type; if that fails (`/api/books/abc`), the client gets `400`.
- `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page` reads `?page=2`. A parameter is required unless it has a default, `required = false`, or type `Optional`.
- `@RequestHeader` reads a header.

Return an ordinary object, a `List`, or a record: Jackson turns record components into JSON fields. To choose the status code and headers yourself, return `ResponseEntity<T>`: `ResponseEntity.ok(book)` or `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()`.

Keep controllers thin: turn the HTTP request into a call on a `@Service`, and its result back into a response. Business rules hidden in controllers are hard to test and reuse.

Tomcat handles each request on a thread taken from a pool of reusable threads, so many threads may run the same controller at once. Controllers must therefore be stateless, like all singleton beans.
takeaways: `@RestController` methods return objects that are turned into JSON
`@PathVariable` binds parts of the path, `@RequestParam` the query string
Return `ResponseEntity` to choose status codes and headers
Keep controllers thin; hand the work to services
pitfalls: Returning null for a missing resource, which gives 200 with an empty body instead of 404.

quiz.q: A method has @RequestParam int page with no default and the request has no page parameter. What happens?
options: The request fails with 400 Bad Request
quiz.explain: Request parameters are required by default; a missing one is a client error unless a default or required = false is set.

concepts.name: Request bodies and status codes
concepts.summary: Accept JSON with @RequestBody, answer 201 Created with a Location header, and handle PUT and DELETE.
concepts.why: Creating and changing data is half of every REST API.
concepts.body:
For `POST`, `PUT` and `PATCH`, the client sends JSON in the request body. Annotate a parameter with `@RequestBody` and Jackson turns that JSON into your Java type (deserializing). Records work well here: immutable, short, and the JSON names match the component names. JSON fields your type doesn't have are ignored by default; text that isn't valid JSON gives `400`.

Use separate **DTOs** (data transfer objects: simple classes or records that only carry data into and out of the API) instead of exposing your database classes directly. That stops clients from setting fields like `id` or `createdAt`, and lets the API and the database change independently.

Status codes matter:

- `201 Created` with a `Location` header (the new item's URL) after creating something: `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto)`. `ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest().path("/{id}")` builds that URL.
- `204 No Content` after a delete, or an update that returns nothing: `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()`, or annotate the method with `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)`.
- `404` when the item doesn't exist, `409` (Conflict) when the request clashes with the current state, such as a duplicate.

`PUT` replaces a whole item and should be **idempotent**: sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once. `PATCH` changes only part of an item. Using each method for its intended job lets clients, and tools that store or resend requests automatically, behave predictably.

Test quickly with `curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}'`, or with the HTTP client built into your IDE.
takeaways: `@RequestBody` turns JSON into a DTO (records work well)
Use separate request and response DTOs instead of database classes
Answer 201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, 404 when missing
pitfalls: Binding request bodies straight to database entities, letting clients overwrite ids or internal fields.

quiz.q: Which response best fits a successful POST that created a resource?
options: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource
quiz.explain: 201 with Location tells the client the resource was created and where to find it.

concepts.name: Spring Data JPA repositories
concepts.summary: Map classes to database tables with JPA, and get ready-made save, find and delete methods and queries from repository interfaces.
concepts.why: Most Spring Boot services store their data in a relational database through Spring Data JPA.
concepts.body:
Most services keep their data in a **relational database** such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, which stores data in tables. Each **row** is one item, say one book. Each **column** is one field of it, such as title or author.

Programs read and change that data in **SQL**, the databases' own language. Each such request is a **query**, like `select * from book where author = 'Herbert'`.

Writing SQL by hand for every class is tedious. **JPA** (Jakarta Persistence) is Java's standard for mapping classes to tables: you save and load objects, and it writes the SQL. A tool that does this is an **ORM** (object-relational mapper). Boot uses Hibernate as its JPA tool, and **Spring Data JPA** on top removes even more code.

Add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` plus the database's **JDBC driver**, the library that lets Java talk to that particular database (H2 is a small built-in database for experiments). Set `spring.datasource.url`, username and password, and Boot sets up the rest, including a **connection pool**: open database connections kept and reused, because opening one is slow.

An **entity** is a class annotated `@Entity`; each object is one row. Mark the identifying field `@Id`, usually with `@GeneratedValue` so the database picks the value. Other fields map to columns; `@Column`, `@Table` and links between entities (`@ManyToOne`, `@OneToMany`) adjust the mapping. Entities need a no-argument constructor (it may be `protected`) and are ordinary mutable classes, not records.

A **repository** is just an interface: `interface BookRepository extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> {}`. At startup Spring writes the class for you, with the **CRUD** operations (create, read, update, delete): `save`, `findById` (returns `Optional`), `findAll`, `deleteById`, `count`, plus paging and sorting.

**Derived queries** come from method names, such as `findByAuthor(String a)` or `countByPublishedAfter(LocalDate d)`. A typo in the name fails at startup, not later. For complex cases write `@Query("select b from Book b where ...")` in **JPQL**, a SQL-like language using class and field names.

The table layout is the database **schema**. Boot creates tables automatically only for built-in databases like H2. For real ones, change the schema with numbered scripts, **database migrations**, run by Flyway or Liquibase, and set `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` to `validate` or `none`.
takeaways: `@Entity` + `@Id` maps a class to a table
Extend `JpaRepository<T, ID>` and get CRUD, paging and sorting for free
Derived query methods are built from their names and checked at startup
Change the schema with Flyway or Liquibase migrations, not ddl-auto
pitfalls: Using spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update on the live database: it can't handle renames and lets the schema drift silently.

quiz.q: What does Spring Data do with a method List<Book> findByAuthor(String author) in a repository interface?
options: Generates a query filtering on the author field
Calls a stored procedure named findByAuthor
quiz.explain: Derived queries are built from the method name, here: where author = the given value.

concepts.name: Testing with @SpringBootTest and @WebMvcTest
concepts.summary: Write unit tests without Spring, slice tests for controllers with MockMvc, and full integration tests.
concepts.why: Fast, focused tests are what make Spring applications safe to change.
concepts.body:
`spring-boot-starter-test` brings JUnit 5, AssertJ (readable assertions), Mockito and Spring's test support. Use three kinds of test.

**Plain unit tests** for services. Because dependencies arrive through the constructor, `new SignupService(fakeNotifier, clock)` needs no Spring at all. These are the fastest, and should be most of your tests.

**Slice tests** start only one layer of the app. `@WebMvcTest(BookController.class)` starts just the web layer plus that controller, and gives you **MockMvc**, which sends requests to it without a real server.

The controller's dependencies are replaced with **mocks**: fake objects whose answers you program in the test with **Mockito**. Declare one with `@MockitoBean` (it replaced the older `@MockBean`). `@DataJpaTest` likewise starts only the database layer, with a built-in test database, and undoes each test's changes afterwards.

**Integration tests** with `@SpringBootTest` start the whole application, checking that all the parts work together. Add `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` to run a real server on a free port, and call it with `TestRestTemplate` or `WebTestClient`.

MockMvc checks the status, headers and JSON of a response: `jsonPath("$.title").value("Dune")` picks the `title` field out of the body. Spring reuses an already started application between tests with the same setup, so keep test setups alike to avoid slow restarts.

Name tests after behaviour. Test the HTTP side (status codes, input checks, JSON shape) at the controller layer, and business rules at the service layer.
takeaways: Unit-test services with plain `new`; no Spring needed
`@WebMvcTest` + MockMvc tests controllers without a server
`@MockitoBean` swaps a bean for a Mockito mock
`@SpringBootTest` starts everything; use it sparingly
pitfalls: Using @SpringBootTest for every test, making the suite slow when slices or plain unit tests would do.

quiz.q: What does @WebMvcTest(BookController.class) load?
options: The entire application including the database
Nothing; it's a plain JUnit test
Only the MVC layer and BookController; other beans must be mocked
quiz.explain: It's a slice test: the web layer and the named controller, with the controller's dependencies supplied as mocks.

concepts.name: Validating input
concepts.summary: Validate request bodies and parameters with Jakarta Bean Validation annotations and @Valid.
concepts.why: Rejecting bad input at the edge keeps invalid data out of your services and database.
concepts.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-validation`, which brings Hibernate Validator, the standard implementation of Jakarta Bean Validation. Then put **constraints** (rules a value must meet) on DTO fields or record components: `@NotBlank`, `@NotNull`, `@Size(max = 100)`, `@Email`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Positive`, `@Past`, `@Pattern(regexp = ...)`. In Boot 3 they come from `jakarta.validation.constraints` (older code used `javax`).

Trigger validation by annotating the controller parameter with `@Valid` (or `@Validated`): `create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUser req)`. If a constraint fails, the method isn't called and Spring throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which becomes a **400 Bad Request**. Customise the response body with an exception handler (next lesson).

Nested objects are validated only if the field itself is annotated `@Valid`. For `@PathVariable` and `@RequestParam` constraints (`@Min(1) @PathVariable long id`), Spring MVC 6.1+ applies method validation automatically when constraints are present.

Write custom constraints when the built-ins aren't enough: an annotation plus a `ConstraintValidator` class. Cross-field rules (end after start) can be a constraint on the class.

Validation in the web layer complements, but doesn't replace, database constraints and business-rule checks in services. You can also validate service methods with `@Validated` on the class, and `@ConfigurationProperties` classes the same way.
takeaways: Constraints like `@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Size` live in `jakarta.validation`
`@Valid` on the parameter triggers validation; failures give 400
Cascade into nested objects with `@Valid` on the field
Validation at the edge complements database constraints
pitfalls: Forgetting @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter, so all the constraint annotations are silently ignored.

quiz.q: A record has @NotBlank String name but the controller parameter is just @RequestBody CreateUser req. What happens with an empty name?
options: The request is accepted; nothing triggers validation
The name is set to null
quiz.explain: Constraints are only checked when validation is triggered, e.g. by @Valid on the parameter.

concepts.name: Error handling and ProblemDetail
concepts.summary: Turn exceptions into consistent HTTP error responses with @RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandler and the ProblemDetail standard format.
concepts.why: Consistent error responses make APIs predictable for clients and keep controllers clean.
concepts.body:
When a controller throws, Spring looks for an **exception handler**. Methods annotated `@ExceptionHandler(SomeException.class)` in a `@RestControllerAdvice` class apply to all controllers, so error handling lives in one place and controllers only deal with the happy path.

Spring supports Problem Details, an internet standard for error bodies (RFC 9457, formerly RFC 7807), through the `ProblemDetail` class. It produces `application/problem+json` bodies with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, plus fields of your own. Set `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` so Spring's own errors (400s for bad input, 405 wrong method, 415 wrong content type) come back in this format too.

A typical setup:

- Define domain exceptions like `BookNotFoundException`.
- Map each to a status in the advice: `ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage())`.
- Extend `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` to customise Spring's built-in exceptions, for example to list validation errors from `MethodArgumentNotValidException`.
- Add a catch-all `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` that writes the error to the log and returns a generic 500, without revealing stack traces to clients.

Alternatively throw `ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "...")` directly for simple cases, or annotate an exception class with `@ResponseStatus`. Unhandled errors fall through to Boot's `/error` endpoint, which returns a basic JSON body.
takeaways: `@RestControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler` centralise error mapping
Return `ProblemDetail` for standard application/problem+json bodies
Map domain exceptions to statuses; never leak stack traces
`ResponseStatusException` covers simple one-off cases
pitfalls: Catching exceptions in every controller method and building error responses by hand, inconsistently.

quiz.q: Where should a handler live so it applies to exceptions from all controllers?
quiz.explain: @ControllerAdvice/@RestControllerAdvice handlers apply globally across controllers.

concepts.name: Typed configuration and profiles
concepts.summary: Bind groups of settings to validated @ConfigurationProperties records and switch environments with profiles.
concepts.why: Typed, validated configuration catches mistakes at startup instead of in production traffic.
concepts.body:
For a group of related settings, define a class or record annotated `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")`. Boot binds `app.mail.host`, `app.mail.port`, `app.mail.from` and nested objects, lists, maps and `Duration`s (`timeout=5s`) to it, converting the text values to the right Java types, and you inject it like any bean. Register it with `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` on the main class or `@EnableConfigurationProperties(MailProperties.class)`.

Benefits over scattered `@Value`s: one place for related settings, IDE auto-completion (with the `spring-boot-configuration-processor` dependency), and **validation** at startup with `@Validated` plus constraints: a missing mail server address stops startup with a clear message.

A **profile** is a named set of settings for one environment, such as `dev` or `prod`. `application-dev.properties` and `application-prod.properties` are loaded in addition to `application.properties` when the `dev` or `prod` profile is active, and override it. Activate with `spring.profiles.active=prod` (often via the environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`). A single YAML file can hold several profile sections separated by `---` with `spring.config.activate.on-profile`.

Beans can be profile-specific with `@Profile("dev")`, for example a fake payment gateway in development. Keep profiles few and about environments; feature switches belong in normal properties.
takeaways: `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a prefix to a typed record or class
`@Validated` + constraints fail fast at startup
`application-{profile}.properties` overrides the defaults for that profile
Activate profiles with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`
pitfalls: Creating a profile per on/off feature switch, leading to endless combinations; use plain properties for switches.

quiz.q: The dev profile is active. application.properties sets app.mail.host=a and application-dev.properties sets it to b. What is bound?
quiz.explain: Profile-specific files are loaded after the default file and override its values.

concepts.name: Transactions with @Transactional
concepts.summary: Group database changes into all-or-nothing units with @Transactional, and understand rollback rules and propagation.
concepts.why: Without correct transaction boundaries, a failure halfway through leaves data half-updated.
concepts.body:
A **transaction** groups several database changes so they all happen or none do. Think of a bank transfer: taking money from one account and adding it to another must never half-happen. Undoing the changes when something fails is a **rollback**.

Annotate a service method with `@Transactional` and Spring starts a transaction before the method and commits (saves for good) after it returns. If it throws, the transaction is rolled back. Everything the method does through repositories, and anything it calls on the same thread, shares that transaction and its database connection.

Rules that matter:

- By default only **unchecked** exceptions (`RuntimeException`, `Error`) trigger rollback. A checked exception commits unless you add `rollbackFor = Exception.class`.
- Inside a transaction, loaded entities are **managed**: change a field and Hibernate writes it at commit (**dirty checking**), no `save` call needed.
- `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on methods that only read lets Hibernate skip dirty checking, and lets some setups send the work to a read-only copy of the database.
- **Propagation** decides what happens when a transactional method calls another: the default `REQUIRED` joins the existing transaction; `REQUIRES_NEW` pauses it and starts an independent one. That suits an audit record (a note of who did what) that must be saved even if the outer work fails.

Transactions work through **proxies**: other beans don't get your object itself but a stand-in wrapped around it, which starts and ends the transaction around each call. So the annotation only works when the method is called from another bean. A call from one method to another in the **same class** skips the proxy, and the inner method's annotation is ignored. Annotated methods should be public (Spring 6 also handles protected and package-private methods with class-based proxies).

Put transaction boundaries on service methods that represent one use case, not on controllers or repositories.
takeaways: `@Transactional` commits on return and rolls back on unchecked exceptions
Checked exceptions commit unless `rollbackFor` says otherwise
`REQUIRED` joins, `REQUIRES_NEW` starts an independent transaction
Self-invocation bypasses the proxy and the annotation
pitfalls: Calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class and expecting a new transaction.

quiz.q: A @Transactional method throws a checked IOException. What happens by default?
quiz.explain: Default rollback rules only cover unchecked exceptions; use rollbackFor to include checked ones.

concepts.name: Calling HTTP APIs with RestClient
concepts.summary: Call other services' web APIs with the fluent RestClient and with annotated HTTP interfaces.
concepts.why: Services constantly call other services and outside web APIs.
concepts.body:
Sometimes your app is the client: it calls another server's web API. **RestClient**, added in Spring Framework 6.1, is the **HTTP client** for this: code that sends requests and reads responses. It is **synchronous**: each call waits for the response before your code continues. It replaces `RestTemplate` for new code (`RestTemplate` still works but gets no new features).

Spring Boot provides a ready `RestClient.Builder` bean that uses the app's JSON settings. Inject it, set a base URL and defaults, and build a client:

```java
RestClient client = builder.baseUrl("https://api.example.com").build();
```

A call reads like the HTTP request: `client.get().uri("/users/{id}", id).retrieve().body(User.class)`. Use `toEntity` to get the status and headers too, `body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<User>>() {})` for generic types, and `.post().body(dto)` to send JSON.

By default a 4xx or 5xx response throws `RestClientResponseException` (`HttpClientErrorException` or `HttpServerErrorException`). Handle it your own way with `onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError, (req, res) -> ...)`.

**HTTP interfaces** are a shorter alternative: write a Java interface whose methods are annotated like `@GetExchange("/users/{id}")`, and let `HttpServiceProxyFactory` generate the implementation, backed by a `RestClient`. The interface reads like a contract and is easy to replace with a fake in tests.

Always set **timeouts**, limits on how long to wait to connect and for an answer, for example with `ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings` or the `spring.http.client.*` properties in recent Boot versions. A call to a slow service with no limit can hold a thread forever. (Apps built on Spring WebFlux use `WebClient` instead.)
takeaways: RestClient is the modern synchronous client; RestTemplate gets no new features
Inject Boot's `RestClient.Builder` to reuse its JSON setup
4xx/5xx throw by default; handle them with `onStatus`
Always set connect and read timeouts
pitfalls: Calling `RestClient.create()` everywhere, losing Boot's JSON settings, metrics and timeouts.

quiz.q: What happens by default when retrieve().body(User.class) receives a 404?
quiz.explain: retrieve() treats 4xx and 5xx statuses as errors and throws unless onStatus handles them.

concepts.name: Actuator: health, metrics and info
concepts.summary: Expose health checks, metrics and runtime information for running the app, with Spring Boot Actuator.
concepts.why: Live systems need health checks, measurements and diagnostics; Actuator provides them out of the box.
concepts.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and the app gains management endpoints under `/actuator`. Only `health` is reachable over HTTP by default; expose more on purpose with `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus`.

A **health check** is a request that tools send regularly to ask "are you working?"; a **metric** is a number tracked over time, like requests per second or memory used. Actuator supplies both.

Key endpoints:

- `/actuator/health` combines **health indicators**, small checks of each thing the app depends on (database, free disk space, Redis), into one UP or DOWN answer. Boot adds an indicator for each such dependency it finds. `management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized` shows the details to logged-in users.
- On **Kubernetes**, a system that runs containers and restarts broken ones, `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` are turned on automatically for its checks.
- `/actuator/metrics` lists **Micrometer** metrics: JVM memory and garbage collection, HTTP request timings (`http.server.requests`), database connections in use. Adding `micrometer-registry-prometheus` exposes `/actuator/prometheus` for **Prometheus**, a monitoring system that collects these numbers regularly.
- `/actuator/info` shows build and git information when configured; `loggers` changes how much the app logs while it runs; `env`, `beans`, `mappings`, `configprops` and `threaddump` help when tracking down problems.

Record your own metrics by injecting `MeterRegistry` and creating counters and timers, or put `@Observed` on a method to time it and count its calls. Write a custom `HealthIndicator` bean to report on something Boot doesn't know about.

Endpoints like `env` and `heapdump` reveal sensitive data. Move management to its own port (`management.server.port`) that a **firewall**, a filter that blocks outside network traffic, keeps private, or protect it with Spring Security.
takeaways: Actuator adds /actuator endpoints; only health is exposed by default
Health indicators are added for each dependency Boot finds
Micrometer metrics can be sent to Prometheus and other systems
Protect or isolate the management endpoints
pitfalls: Exposing all endpoints (include=*) on the public port, leaking settings, passwords and memory dumps.

quiz.q: Which endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default after adding Actuator?
quiz.explain: Spring Boot exposes only the health endpoint over HTTP by default; others must be included explicitly.

concepts.name: Securing APIs with Spring Security
concepts.summary: Configure a SecurityFilterChain to check who callers are and what they may do, including APIs that accept JWT tokens.
concepts.why: Every real API must check who is calling and what they may do, and Spring Security is the standard way.
concepts.body:
Two questions protect an API: who is calling (**authentication**, like checking ID at a door) and what they may do (**authorization**). Adding `spring-boot-starter-security` secures **everything** at once: every endpoint requires a login, with a generated password printed at startup, plus HTTP Basic (username and password sent with each request) and a login form. That's a safe default; you then open up what you actually want.

Security runs as a chain of filters: small checks that every request passes through before reaching your controllers, each able to reject it. Configure the chain by declaring a **SecurityFilterChain** bean, built with lambdas on `HttpSecurity`:

- `authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll().requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE).hasRole("ADMIN").anyRequest().authenticated())` sets rules per URL, checked in order.
- `httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())`, `formLogin(...)` or `oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))` choose how callers prove who they are.

APIs called by other programs usually send a **token** with each request instead of logging in: a signed string proving who the caller is. Such an API keeps no login state, so switch off server-side **sessions** (the server remembering a logged-in user between requests) with `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`. Protection against **CSRF**, an attack that abuses a browser's automatic login **cookies** (small values a website stores in the browser), can then be switched off too.

A **JWT** (JSON Web Token) is the common token format: signed JSON saying who the user is and when the token expires. With a resource server (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server`), set `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri`, and Spring checks every request's JWT against your **identity provider**, the service that logs users in (Keycloak, Auth0, Entra ID).

Method-level rules use `@EnableMethodSecurity` and `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.name")`. Inject the current user with `@AuthenticationPrincipal`. Store passwords only as hashes made by a `PasswordEncoder` such as BCrypt. Test with `@WithMockUser` or the `jwt()` request helper.
takeaways: Adding the starter secures everything; then you open up on purpose
Configure a `SecurityFilterChain` bean with lambdas
Request rules are checked in order; put specific rules first
A resource server checks each request's JWT against the identity provider
pitfalls: Switching off CSRF protection in an app where browsers log in with session cookies, opening it to cross-site request forgery.

quiz.q: Rules are .anyRequest().authenticated() followed by .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll(). What happens?
options: It fails: anyRequest() must be the last rule
quiz.explain: Matchers are evaluated in order; Spring Security rejects configurations with rules after anyRequest().

concepts.name: How auto-configuration works
concepts.summary: Conditional configuration classes, @ConditionalOnMissingBean and the conditions report.
concepts.why: Knowing how Boot decides what to set up lets you override defaults confidently and find out why startup did something.
concepts.body:
Auto-configuration is ordinary Spring configuration that Boot applies **conditionally**. Each auto-configuration class is listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` inside the Boot JARs (and in starters from other projects). At startup Boot loads the list and evaluates each class's conditions:

- `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)`: only if a class is on the classpath. This is why adding a starter "turns on" a feature.
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`: only if you haven't defined your own bean of that type. This is how your configuration wins: Boot's bean steps aside.
- `@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "app.cache", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true")`: driven by configuration.
- `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`, `@ConditionalOnBean`, `@ConditionalOnResource` and more.

Auto-configurations are processed **after** your own configuration, so the conditions see your beans. Ordering between them uses `@AutoConfiguration(after = ...)`.

To customise, you rarely replace beans; first look for properties (`spring.jackson.*`) or **customizer** beans (`Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer`, `WebServerFactoryCustomizer`). Defining your own `ObjectMapper` or `DataSource` bean makes Boot's version step aside entirely. Exclude an auto-configuration with `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` or `spring.autoconfigure.exclude`.

To investigate, start with `--debug` (or `debug=true`): the conditions evaluation report lists positive and negative matches with reasons. The `/actuator/conditions` endpoint shows the same at runtime.
takeaways: Auto-configurations are conditional `@Configuration` classes listed in `AutoConfiguration.imports`
`@ConditionalOnClass` reacts to the classpath; `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` lets your beans win
Prefer properties and customizer beans over replacing auto-configured beans
`--debug` prints the conditions evaluation report
pitfalls: Defining your own ObjectMapper bean to change one setting and losing all of Boot's Jackson configuration.

quiz.q: You define your own DataSource bean. What does DataSourceAutoConfiguration do?
options: Wraps your bean in a proxy
quiz.explain: Auto-configured beans are conditional on the absence of a user-defined bean of the same type.

concepts.name: JPA performance: N+1, fetching and projections
concepts.summary: Detect and fix N+1 queries, choose when related data loads, and read data efficiently with projections and paging.
concepts.why: JPA hides SQL, and the queries it generates by default are the most common Spring performance problem.
concepts.body:
The **N+1 problem**: you load N orders with one query, then touching `order.getCustomer()` for each one fires N more queries. It's invisible in the code and painful on the live system. Make it visible first: turn on `spring.jpa.show-sql` or, better, log `org.hibernate.SQL` at DEBUG level and count queries in tests.

When related data loads:

- `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` links are *eager* by default in JPA: the related object loads right away with its parent. Mark them `fetch = FetchType.LAZY` so it loads only when first used. Collections (`@OneToMany`) are lazy already.
- Load what a use case needs in one query with a **fetch join**, `select o from Order o join fetch o.customer`, or `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer")` on a repository method.
- `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` (e.g. 50) groups lazy loads into `IN (...)` queries of many ids at once, as a safety net.

Spring Boot turns on **open-in-view** by default: the database session stays open until the web response is written, so lazy loads still work inside controllers, and Boot prints a warning about it at startup. Set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` so a lazy load outside a transaction fails loudly instead of firing hidden queries.

For read-only screens, query **projections** instead of entities: a record or interface with just the needed columns (`List<BookSummary> findByAuthor(String a)`), which skips dirty-checking overhead. Page large results with `Pageable` (`findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("title")))`). Fetch-joining collections while paging forces Hibernate to page in memory instead of in the database, so avoid that combination.
takeaways: N+1: one query for the list plus one per item; count queries to catch it
Make to-one links LAZY and fetch per use case with join fetch or @EntityGraph
Turn off open-in-view so hidden lazy loading fails fast
Use projections and paging for read-heavy endpoints
pitfalls: Leaving @ManyToOne eager, so every load of the entity pulls related rows you didn't need.

quiz.q: Loading 100 orders and reading order.getCustomer().getName() in a loop issues 101 queries. What fixes it in one query?
options: A join fetch or @EntityGraph on the query
quiz.explain: A fetch join (or entity graph) loads orders and customers together in a single SQL statement.

concepts.name: Integration tests with Testcontainers
concepts.summary: Run tests against real databases and brokers in Docker with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection.
concepts.why: Tests against H2 miss behaviour of the real database; Testcontainers makes testing against the real thing cheap.
concepts.body:
Built-in test databases such as H2 behave differently from PostgreSQL or MySQL (SQL details, constraints, JSON columns, locking), so tests pass and the live system fails. **Testcontainers** starts real services in throwaway Docker containers during tests, and removes them afterwards.

Spring Boot supports it directly. Add `spring-boot-testcontainers` and the Testcontainers library for your service (`org.testcontainers:postgresql`), then declare the container as a bean or static field annotated `@ServiceConnection`. Boot reads the container's address, port and login details and sets up the database connection (or Kafka, Redis, MongoDB, RabbitMQ) automatically, with no extra setup code.

Common setups:

- Annotate a test class with `@Testcontainers` and a `static @Container @ServiceConnection PostgreSQLContainer<?>` field; the container starts once for the class.
- Share containers across test classes: put `@Bean @ServiceConnection` definitions in a `@TestConfiguration` class and import it, so Spring reuses one started application with its containers.
- Combine with `@DataJpaTest` and `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` for fast repository tests against the real database, running your Flyway migrations.

The same setup works at **development time**: a `TestApplication` main in `src/test` that calls `SpringApplication.from(App::main).with(ContainersConfig.class).run(args)` starts the app with its containers, replacing hand-written Docker Compose files (Docker's format for starting several containers together). Boot also reads Docker Compose files directly with `spring-boot-docker-compose`.
takeaways: Testcontainers runs real dependencies in Docker for tests
`@ServiceConnection` sets up the connection details automatically
Put containers in a shared `@TestConfiguration` to reuse them
The same setup can run the app locally
pitfalls: Starting a new container in every test class without sharing, making the suite slow.

quiz.q: What does @ServiceConnection on a PostgreSQLContainer bean do?
options: Tells Boot to derive DataSource connection details from the container
Starts PostgreSQL on the host machine
quiz.explain: Boot creates connection details from the running container, replacing manual spring.datasource properties.

concepts.name: Scheduling, async and virtual threads
concepts.summary: Run jobs on a timer with @Scheduled, run work in the background with @Async, and handle more blocking work with virtual threads.
concepts.why: Background work and many requests at once are part of most services, and Java 21 changes how you scale them.
concepts.body:
**Scheduling** runs a method on a timer. Add `@EnableScheduling` to a configuration class and annotate methods with `@Scheduled(fixedRate = 60_000)` (every minute), `fixedDelay` (wait that long after the previous run finishes), or `cron = "0 0 3 * * *"`, a cron expression: a compact schedule format from Unix, which in Spring has six fields starting with seconds. `fixedRateString = "PT1M"` or `${...}` placeholders keep schedules configurable. If the app runs as several copies at once, every copy runs every job; use a lock library such as ShedLock, or a dedicated scheduler, for jobs that must run once.

**Async methods**: `@EnableAsync` plus `@Async` on a bean method runs it on another thread from a task executor, and the caller carries on immediately. Return `void` or `CompletableFuture<T>`. It works through a **proxy** (a stand-in Spring wraps around the bean), so a call from the same class runs on the caller's own thread instead. Boot sets up the executor (`spring.task.execution.pool.*`).

**Virtual threads** (Java 21+): set `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` and Boot runs Tomcat's request handling, `@Async` tasks and scheduled tasks on virtual threads. A call that waits, such as a database query or a RestClient call, then no longer holds one of the few platform threads, so a simple service written in the ordinary waiting style handles many more requests at once.

Limits to know: the database connection pool still caps how much database work runs at once; `synchronized` blocks around waiting calls can pin carrier threads on JDK 21 to 23 (fixed in JDK 24); and pure calculation gains nothing.
takeaways: `@Scheduled` with fixedRate, fixedDelay or a six-field cron expression
`@Async` runs bean methods on an executor; return CompletableFuture
`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` moves request handling to virtual threads
Every running copy runs scheduled jobs; lock if they must run once
pitfalls: Calling an @Async method from the same class and wondering why it doesn't run in the background.

quiz.q: What does the Spring cron expression "0 */15 * * * *" mean?
quiz.explain: Spring cron has six fields starting with seconds, so this fires at second 0 of every 15th minute.

concepts.name: Bean lifecycle, proxies and AOP
concepts.summary: How Spring creates beans, where BeanPostProcessors and proxies come in, and why calls within the same class skip them.
concepts.why: Most baffling Spring bugs (annotations ignored, beans in odd states) come from lifecycle and proxy details.
concepts.body:
Creating a bean goes through defined phases: the application context reads **bean definitions** (descriptions of which beans to create) (from scanning, `@Bean` methods, auto-configuration), lets `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`s modify the definitions (this is how `${...}` placeholders are resolved), then for each singleton: instantiate, inject dependencies, run **Aware** callbacks (methods through which Spring hands the bean framework objects it asked for), call `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization`, run init callbacks (`@PostConstruct`, `afterPropertiesSet`), then `postProcessAfterInitialization`. On shutdown, `@PreDestroy` runs.

That last post-processing step is where **proxies** are created. Features like `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable`, `@Validated`, `@PreAuthorize` and custom `@Aspect`s are **AOP** (aspect-oriented programming: adding behaviour around many methods from one place). A post-processor wraps the bean in a proxy that runs the extra behaviour around method calls. Spring Boot uses CGLIB subclass proxies by default; JDK dynamic proxies are used only for interface-based proxying when configured.

Consequences:

- **Self-invocation**: `this.other()` inside the bean calls the target directly, not the proxy, so `other()`'s annotations do nothing. Restructure into a separate bean.
- CGLIB proxies can't intercept `final` or `private` methods, and a `final` class can't be proxied at all.
- The object injected elsewhere is the proxy, not your instance; `getClass()` shows a `$$SpringCGLIB$$` subclass.

Bean **scopes** other than singleton (`prototype`, `request`, `session`) also use proxies when injected into singletons. `@Configuration` classes are themselves CGLIB-enhanced so that calling one `@Bean` method from another returns the singleton; `proxyBeanMethods = false` turns this off for faster startup.
takeaways: BeanPostProcessors run around init callbacks; proxies are created after initialisation
Transactions, async, caching and security are proxy-based AOP
Self-invocation, final and private methods bypass proxies
`@Configuration` classes are proxied so @Bean methods return singletons
pitfalls: Marking a @Transactional or @Cacheable method private or final, so the proxy can't intercept it.

quiz.q: Why is helper()'s @Timed ignored when build() calls this.helper()?
options: @Timed only works on the first method
The call goes to the target object directly, bypassing the proxy
Aspects don't work on public methods
quiz.explain: Only calls coming through the proxy are intercepted; this.helper() is a plain Java call on the target.

concepts.name: Writing your own starter
concepts.summary: Bundle shared setup as your own starter: auto-configuration classes with conditions, typed settings and IDE hints.
concepts.why: Platform teams share logging, security and client setup across dozens of services through internal starters.
concepts.body:
When several services need the same setup (an HTTP client for an internal API, audit logging, a security baseline), package it as a **starter** so each service adds one dependency and gets sensible defaults it can override.

The usual structure is two separate build projects (Maven or Gradle modules):

- `acme-audit-spring-boot-autoconfigure`: the `@AutoConfiguration` classes, `@ConfigurationProperties`, and the registration file `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` listing them, one fully qualified class name per line.
- `acme-audit-spring-boot-starter`: an empty jar whose POM depends on the autoconfigure module and the libraries it needs. Starters not made by the Spring team are named `xxx-spring-boot-starter`; the `spring-boot-starter-*` prefix is reserved for official ones.

Design rules:

- Guard everything with conditions: `@ConditionalOnClass` for optional libraries, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on every bean so applications can replace it, `@ConditionalOnProperty` for an on/off switch.
- Expose settings through a prefixed `@ConfigurationProperties` class and include `spring-boot-configuration-processor` so IDEs suggest them as you type.
- Don't component-scan inside auto-configuration; declare beans explicitly. Use `@AutoConfiguration(after = ...)` to order relative to Boot's own.

Test it with `ApplicationContextRunner`, which starts tiny contexts in milliseconds and lets you assert which beans exist under different properties and classpaths (`FilteredClassLoader`).
takeaways: Split into an autoconfigure module and an empty starter POM
Register classes in `AutoConfiguration.imports`; don't rely on scanning
Make every bean `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` so apps can override
Test with `ApplicationContextRunner`
pitfalls: Naming an internal starter spring-boot-starter-foo, the prefix reserved for official Spring Boot starters.

quiz.q: How does Spring Boot discover your auto-configuration class in a starter jar?
quiz.explain: Boot loads auto-configuration class names from AutoConfiguration.imports files on the classpath.

concepts.name: Native images, AOT and startup tuning
concepts.summary: Compile Spring Boot apps ahead of time into GraalVM native images, and speed up normal JVM startup with CDS.
concepts.why: Fast startup and low memory matter when apps start on demand or many copies share one machine in containers.
concepts.body:
A Spring app normally finds beans, checks conditions and creates proxies at startup, using reflection, which takes time. Spring's **AOT** (ahead-of-time) processing moves that work to build time: it starts the application context in a special mode, then generates Java code for the bean definitions, plus **hints** listing which classes, files and proxies must be available when the app runs.

A GraalVM **native image** goes further: it compiles the app and the needed parts of the JDK into one program the operating system runs directly, with no JVM. It relies on a closed-world assumption: everything the app can reach must be known at build time. With the GraalVM Native Build Tools plugin, `./mvnw -Pnative native:compile` (or `./gradlew nativeCompile`, or `spring-boot:build-image -Pnative` for a container) builds a program that starts in tens of milliseconds and uses far less memory.

The costs: long builds, top speed often below a warmed-up JVM (whose JIT compiler keeps optimizing the busiest code while running), and no changing behaviour at run time.

Restrictions follow from the closed world: the classpath and `@Profile`/`@ConditionalOnProperty` choices are fixed at build time, and reflection, files, proxies and serialization that Spring can't work out need hints via `RuntimeHintsRegistrar` and `@ImportRuntimeHints`, or `@RegisterReflectionForBinding`. Run the tests as a native image too (`-PnativeTest`) to catch missing hints.

Staying on the JVM, **CDS** (Class Data Sharing) cuts startup a lot with no code changes: extract the JAR (`-Djarmode=tools extract`), do one trial run with `-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh` to record the loaded classes, then start with `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa`. Lazy initialisation (`spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`) also helps, but configuration errors then appear later instead of at startup.
takeaways: AOT processing generates bean definitions and runtime hints at build time
Native images start in milliseconds but fix the classpath and conditions at build time
Register hints for reflection and resources Spring can't infer
CDS speeds up JVM startup with no code changes
pitfalls: Relying on a profile or property set at run time to switch beans in a native image; those conditions were decided at build time.

quiz.q: Why does a native image need reflection hints?
options: GraalVM doesn't support reflection at all
Under the closed-world assumption only reflection known at build time is included
quiz.explain: Native image includes only reachable code and metadata; dynamic reflection must be declared ahead of time.
